Immune-Inspired Pattern Recognition for Network Intrusion Traffic

A two-layer negative-selection and clonal-selection system, evaluated on NSL-KDD. November 2026.

1. Executive summary

An artificial immune system (AIS) is worth deploying for this problem as a pattern-memory and triage layer next to a conventional classifier, not as a stand-alone detector. Its clonal-selection memory recognised the five traffic families (normal, DoS, Probe, R2L, U2R) with a macro-F1 of 0.619, against 0.494 for a Random Forest, while storing 863 memory cells instead of about 115,000 tree nodes. When an entire attack family was removed from training, the immune system still flagged 71.8% of the unseen DoS traffic, where the Random Forest flagged 2.1%. Given five labelled examples of the unseen Probe family, it recognised 52.0% of test Probe traffic after a 3 ms update, against 11.7% for a fully retrained Random Forest.

Two results argue against overselling it. First, the system raises more false alarms: the configuration selected on validation flags 7.9% of normal test traffic, against 2.7% for the Random Forest. Second, the textbook negative-selection algorithm fails in the 12-dimensional feature space used here, detecting 3.2% of attacks. It only works after changing where detectors are generated, and even then a one-line nearest-normal-sample rule performs as well. This reproduces the critique by Stibor et al. (2005).

Recommended next steps: lower the false-alarm rate before any pilot (for example with a dendritic-cell context layer), then repeat the evaluation on modern traffic (UNSW-NB15 or CIC-IDS2017), because NSL-KDD is built from 1998 traffic.

2. Choosing the use case

Four candidate applications were compared against the brief (pattern recognition first, cyber security, evidence-backed, implementable now).

CandidateAIS mechanismEvidence in the literatureData available nowDecision
Recognising attack patterns in network connection recordsNegative selection + clonal selectionKim & Bentley (2001) combined both for intrusion detection; Hooks et al. (2018) tested both on NSL-KDD and reported scaling problems worth re-examiningYes: NSL-KDD, with 17 attack types that appear only in the test setSelected
Malware family recognition from API calls or app permissionsAIRS, negative selectionReviewed by Alrubayyi et al. (2021); recent Android work such as YATSIDroid (Mahindru et al., 2026)Needs a malware corpus and feature extractionStrong follow-up
Port-scan and botnet detection from host signalsDendritic cell algorithm (danger theory)Greensmith et al. (2006, 2010) detected port scans with low false-positive ratesNeeds time-windowed live signalsBest candidate to cut false alarms
Spam filteringNegative selectionIdris (2012)YesLow novelty

Network-traffic pattern recognition was chosen because it is a genuine multi-class recognition problem, it lets both main AIS families work together, and its public test set contains 3,750 connections from attack types the training set never shows. That gives an honest test of the property AIS research claims most often: recognising what it has not seen.

3. How the immune system maps to the algorithm

Negative selection: the thymus as a boot camp

The thymus produces T-cells with random receptors, shows every recruit samples of the body's own proteins, and destroys any recruit that reacts. The survivors can only react to things that are not part of the body, so the body has an alarm for invaders it has never met (Forrest et al., 1994). In the algorithm, a detector is a random point in feature space. It survives only if it is far enough from every normal connection, and it is allowed to grow until it touches normal traffic (the V-Detector of Ji & Dasgupta, 2004). Anything that falls inside a detector is non-self.

Figure 1. Negative selection in two dimensions. Normal traffic (blue) forms a ring; red discs are detectors. With a lower coverage target (left) some anomalies fall into holes between detectors.

Clonal selection: a locksmith with a box of keys

When a pathogen appears, the B-cells whose antibodies roughly fit it multiply, and the copies mutate: a close fit is copied carefully, a poor fit is copied with large random changes. Copies that bind better survive and some become long-lived memory cells, so the next encounter is handled faster (de Castro & Von Zuben, 2002). Think of a locksmith shown a new lock. He takes his closest keys, cuts many slightly different copies, and keeps any copy that fits better than the original. The kept keys are the memory cells; a new lock is labelled by the key that fits it best.

Figure 2. Clonal selection on three synthetic pattern classes. Stars are memory cells, before (left) and after (right) ten generations. Grey areas are too far from any memory cell to be recognised.

Concept mapping

Immune conceptWhat it does in the bodyWhat it does in this system
AntigenMolecule presented to the immune systemOne network connection record, mapped into a 12-dimensional shape-space in [0, 1]
SelfThe body's own cellsNormal traffic
Thymic negative selectionDeletes T-cells that react to selfV-Detector: random detector centres whose radius stops at the nearest normal sample
Clonal expansionCells that bind an antigen multiplyThe 3 best-matching memory cells are cloned in proportion to their affinity rank
Somatic hypermutationCopies mutate, less for good bindersGaussian mutation whose step size is proportional to the distance to the antigen
Affinity maturationBetter binders surviveThe best clone replaces the best-matching memory cell if it is closer to the antigen
Receptor editingB-cells swap out unhelpful receptorsMemory cells never stimulated in a generation are replaced by fresh training samples
Activation thresholdBinding must be strong enough to trigger a responsePer-class recognition radius; beyond it the record is 'not recognised'
Secondary responseFaster response to a pathogen seen beforelearn_new_pattern() adds memory cells for a new family without touching existing memory

4. System design

Figure 3. The two-layer immune pattern recognizer.

Think of a hospital reception desk. The receptionist (layer 1, memory) recognises regular patients and known troublemakers on sight. Anyone she does not recognise goes to the security guard (layer 2, negative selection), who has only been taught what staff look like and therefore stops anyone who is not staff, including a stranger nobody has described to him. The people he stops are labelled NOVEL and sent to an analyst, whose labels become new memory.

  • Shape-space. Heavy-tailed counters are log-transformed, the three categorical fields are one-hot encoded, numeric fields are standardised, and PCA keeps 12 components (77.5% of variance), rescaled to [0, 1]. The transform is fitted on training data only.
  • Layer 2, negative selection. V-Detector trained on 8,000 normal connections, self radius 0.01, coverage target 0.99. Candidate detectors are drawn around randomly chosen normal samples (Gaussian, sigma 0.25) rather than uniformly in the cube. This self-proximal sampling follows density-guided variants such as ASD-RNSA (Yang, Chen & Li, 2017); section 6.1 shows why it is needed.
  • Layer 1, clonal-selection memory. CLONALG-style training with a memory budget of 150 cells scaled by the square root of class size (863 cells in total), mutation scale 0.3, 6 generations, 3 cells selected per antigen. An optional negative-selection operator that rejects clones drifting toward other classes (Kim & Bentley, 2001) is implemented; validation preferred it switched off.
  • Decision rule. A record is recognised if it lies within its nearest memory cell's class radius (the 0.99 quantile of training distances). Unrecognised records go to layer 2. Under the selected 'tolerance' policy, records inside a detector are NOVEL and the rest are normal.

5. Data and evaluation protocol

FamilyKDDTrain+KDDTest+
normal67,3439,711
DoS45,9277,458
Probe11,6562,421
R2L9952,887
U2R5267

NSL-KDD (Tavallaee et al., 2009) removes the duplicate records of KDD Cup '99. Its test set includes 17 attack types absent from training (apache2, httptunnel, mailbomb, mscan, named, processtable, ps, saint, sendmail, snmpgetattack, snmpguess, sqlattack, udpstorm, worm, xlock, xsnoop, xterm), 3,750 rows in total. R2L is rare in training (0.8%) but 12.8% of the test set, which makes it the hardest family for every model.

  • KDDTrain+ was split 80/20 (stratified) into fitting (100,778 rows) and validation (25,195 rows) sets. Every hyper-parameter, threshold and decision policy was chosen on validation; KDDTest+ was used only for the reported numbers.
  • Stochastic models were run with 5 seeds (3 for the two-layer system, 2 for the hold-out study). Tables show mean ± standard deviation.
  • Detection rate (DR) is the share of attacks flagged; false-alarm rate (FAR) is the share of normal connections flagged. Macro-F1 averages F1 over the five families, so rare families count as much as common ones.
  • Baselines: Isolation Forest, one-class SVM, LOF, a nearest-normal-sample rule (the 'self detector' of Stibor et al., 2005), 1-nearest-neighbour on all training data, Random Forest (plain and class-balanced), and an ablation that uses the same number of randomly chosen prototypes without affinity maturation.

Table 1. Anomaly detection, trained on normal traffic only, evaluated on KDDTest+. 'Native rule' is each model's own decision rule.

Figure 4. ROC curves on KDDTest+ (first seed for the stochastic models).

Classic V-Detector, with detectors drawn uniformly, stopped after about 18 detectors and caught 3.2% of attacks. Its coverage estimate is fooled: most random points in a 12-dimensional cube are far from all traffic, so large detectors quickly 'cover' empty space while the regions next to normal traffic, where attacks actually sit, stay open. Drawing candidates around normal samples raised the detection rate to 60.1% at a 2.4% false-alarm rate. At that operating point the nearest-normal-sample rule is equivalent (62.0% DR, 2.7% FAR) and ranks connections better overall (AUC 0.953 against 0.825).

Figure 5. Validation detection and false-alarm rates of V-Detector as the shape-space dimension grows.

Figure 5 isolates the cause. Up to 4 dimensions the two samplers perform about the same. From 8 dimensions upward the uniform sampler's detection rate falls to 13 to 29%, while the self-proximal sampler stays between 84% and 97%, at the cost of more detectors (3,000, the cap, at 24 dimensions).

Table 2. Five-family recognition on KDDTest+. Model size is memory cells, stored samples or tree nodes.

Figure 6. Recall per family on KDDTest+ (error bars: standard deviation over seeds).

Accuracy is similar across models (72 to 76%). The difference is in the rare families: the clonal memory recalls 23.4% of R2L and 39.1% of U2R connections, where the Random Forest recalls 0.2% and 6.0%. The forest's errors come from class imbalance (52 U2R training rows against 67,343 normal), and class weighting only partly fixes it (macro-F1 0.541). The ablation shows how much of the gain is due to the immune mechanism itself. Random prototypes with the same per-class budget already reach 0.576, and affinity maturation adds about 0.04 more (0.619). Most of the advantage over the forest therefore comes from a memory with a fixed budget per class; clonal selection improves that memory modestly.

Figure 7. Row-normalised confusion matrix of the clonal memory (first seed).

Table 3. Two-layer recognizer on KDDTest+. q is the recognition quantile; the configuration with the highest validation F1 was selected.

Figure 8. What happens to each test family under the selected configuration. 'Known types' excludes the attack types that appear only in the test set.

The selected configuration detects 72.1% of test attacks against 58.9% for the Random Forest, and 43.2% of the test-only attack types against 19.4%. The negative-selection layer adds to what memory alone achieves (memory alone: 69.3% DR, 33.1% on test-only types). The false-alarm rate is 7.9%, about three times the forest's. On the 9,711 normal test connections that is roughly 766 alerts against 261. Validation F1 hardly separates the six configurations (0.968 to 0.974), while test behaviour differs. A lower quantile with the 'alarm_union' policy reaches 74% DR at 8.0% FAR and labels more of the test-only types as NOVEL. The choice between these settings is an operating decision, best made with analysts' alert budget in mind.

Table 5. Recall of the held-out family after learning from a few labelled examples. The immune system adds memory cells; the Random Forest is retrained on everything.

Figure 9. Secondary response: recall of a newly introduced family against the number of labelled examples.

Without DoS in training, the forest sends almost all DoS traffic to 'normal' (2.1% detected), because a supervised classifier can only choose among the classes it knows. The immune system detects 71.8%, most of it labelled NOVEL, which is the output an analyst can act on. From five labelled Probe examples, the immune memory recalls 52.0% of test Probe traffic against 11.7% for a retrained forest, and the update takes milliseconds instead of about 14 seconds. For DoS the immune memory stays slightly ahead with 20 and 80 examples, though the gap narrows. R2L is the exception: neither system learns it, because the R2L connections in the test set differ from those in training (Divekar et al., 2018, discuss this imbalance and shift).

7. Where the immune analogy helps and where it does not

Claim: negative selection detects unknown attacks. Partly supported. Detection depends on where detectors are placed, not on the biology. A nearest-normal-sample rule, with no detectors at all, matches V-Detector here. Stibor et al. (2005) reached the same conclusion and found real-valued negative selection uncompetitive with statistical methods on KDD data. Gupta & Dasgupta (2021) present the counter-view: in their review, NSA variants do well on non-linear one-class problems and run faster than neural models. In this study negative selection is useful as a cheap second opinion, not as the main detector.

Claim: clonal selection is a better classifier. Weakly supported. Its macro-F1 advantage over Random Forest is real, but most of it comes from storing a balanced memory of prototypes, which random sampling also achieves. Affinity maturation added about 0.04 macro-F1. The memory is also about 117 times smaller than storing every training sample, and every decision can be explained by pointing at the memory cell that matched.

Claim: an immune system adapts to new threats. Supported for DoS and Probe. The system flagged most of a family it never saw and learned it from five examples without forgetting old ones; the unit tests check that old memory is unchanged. It did not help for R2L, whose test traffic looks like normal traffic in this feature space.

The other side. In a security operations centre, false alarms cost analyst time, and the forest's 2.7% false-alarm rate is a strong reason to prefer it as the primary detector. NSL-KDD comes from simulated 1998 traffic; Divekar et al. (2018) recommend newer datasets such as UNSW-NB15, so these numbers should not be read as performance on today's networks.

8. Limitations and next steps

  • False alarms. Add a dendritic-cell layer (Greensmith et al., 2010) that fuses context signals, such as error rates and connection bursts, before an alert is raised. Tune the alert threshold to a fixed analyst budget.
  • Modern data. Repeat E1 to E4 on UNSW-NB15 and CIC-IDS2017, and on a malware dataset (API-call sequences) to cover the malware-detection half of the brief.
  • Learned shape-space. PCA was chosen for simplicity. A metric learned so that attack families separate might help R2L, though it must be fitted without test data.
  • Online operation. Memory updates are already incremental. A streaming version would also need memory cells to age out and periodic re-tolerisation as normal traffic drifts.
  • Robustness. Attackers can shape traffic to sit inside the self region. Adversarial evaluation is untested.

9. Reproducing the results

The code is in the artificial_immune_systems folder (package ais_patrec). From that folder:

  • pip install -r requirements.txt
  • pytest -q (10 unit tests)
  • python experiments/run_experiments.py (about 10 minutes on 2 CPU cores; downloads NSL-KDD on first run)
  • python experiments/make_tables.py (writes results/summary.md)

Every number in this report comes from results/metrics.json produced by that run.
